This is likely due to inaccuracies in the air flow rates which are difficult to measure precisely since there are often significant flow variations through the cross section of the flow chamber, and calibration of the air flow sensors is also known to be challenging. The water side heat transfer is considered to be more accurate and is used to characterize the heat transfer performance of the coils, while the air side heat transfer rates are used only to provide a general verification of the water side rates. The accuracy in the CAV modes (with higher air flow rates that are maintained constant) is more stable and matches the water side heat transfer to within approximately 10%. There are additional uncertainties in the humidity reading (about 5% accuracy), which impacts the air side enthalpy calculation, so the 10% difference and very consistent trends in the data give confidence that the measurements are reasonable. Normalized air and water thermal powers 2.1.1.2 Analysis of Load Metrics Figure 3 shows a comparison of several key performance metrics recorded during the M&V that characterize the HVAC system operation in the different operating modes. It is evident that the different operating modes have quite different characteristics, which consequently result in differences in energy use. A clear difference is apparent in the nature of the zone and supply air temperatures for the VAV HEDS mode compared to the other three modes. The average zone temperature is maintained nearly constant at about 70 °F in modes other than VAV HEDS, while the controls in that mode accept a setback in the range of 67-72 °F. The supply air temperature is a direct result of the dewpoint set point and CRC operation, so the HEDS supply air temperature variations are also a result of the control strategy. Note that the estimated VAV box supply air temperature is calculated based on an energy balance using the HEDS supply air temperature, the VAV reheat coil load and the total air supply flow rate. 4 This report is available at no cost from NREL at www.nrel.gov/publications. Note that the supply air temperatures to the VAV boxes in the VAV HEDS mode is equivalent to the HEDS supply air temperature since there is virtually no VAV reheat required in this operating mode; the HEDS energy recovery system can meet the reheat needs. According to Conservant literature, the reheat coil recovers 20-40% of the energy extracted from the air during the cooling and dehumidification process. The air reheating that occurs using the energy recovery reheat coil (CRC) directly avoids the need to provide reheating through other means, which can reduce or eliminate natural gas use for reheat.
